beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. Last week we attached the question bank to the roadmap, but one whole question type was being thrown away. Concept-matching questions, the match-each-X-to-its-Y kind, have an answer that's a mapping, not a single letter, so the gate couldn't grade them. A hundred eighty-six were skipped in last week's build. This week I made them gradable, and turned them into an optional check-your-knowledge step that can actually let a student skip ahead. The question: how do you let someone prove they know something with a matching question, and have it count, without it ever being a graded test?

beats.narration_text: The answer is a formative knowledge-check, with three properties. One: it's opt-in. A student gets their full roadmap without answering anything; the check only runs if they choose it. Two: it can advance you. If you pass, the gate trusts that prerequisite and skips it, along with what it builds on, the same prune-after-evaluate rule the MCQs use. Three: it's never graded. The pass is recorded as a knowledge-check, never as a grade of record. It can move you forward, but it is not a test.

beats.narration_text: Here's the problem it solves. A matching question asks you to pair each item with the right description, so the answer is a whole mapping, four links, not one letter. The old single-answer gate had no way to read that, so it dropped every matching question in the bank, a hundred eighty-six of them last week. That's a whole question type, across the entire book, going completely unused.

beats.narration_text: So how do you grade a mapping fairly? You score each pair on its own. This is relational partial credit, from the concept-map scoring literature, and for matching items it's the same as per-option partial credit with no negative marking, which the research says separates strong and weak learners best. The score is simply the number of correct pairs over the number of prompts. Match three of four and you score seventy-five percent. The pass bar is seventy-five percent by default, and that sits well above chance, since getting a four-by-four match completely right by luck is only about four percent.

beats.narration_text: One honest subtlety. A hundred fifty-seven of these are four-by-four bijections, four prompts, four options, each used once. There you can't miss exactly one, getting three right forces the fourth, so seventy-five percent is actually unreachable, and the bar means a perfect answer. The other twenty-two have a spare distractor option, so they can land on real partial credit like two out of three. It's an asymmetry worth naming, and faculty can lower the bar if near-perfect is too strict.

beats.narration_text: In the gate it behaves just like the other items. Match all four and you advance, the prerequisite is pruned. Match two of four and you remediate, it stays in your plan. Opt out entirely and nothing changes, you just keep it. Every result is recorded as a knowledge-check, never as a grade. A pass can move where your roadmap begins, but it never goes on a transcript.

beats.narration_text: Here's what the student sees. Match each organelle to its function, with a dropdown per prompt. On a pass, four of four, every pair turns green, and it says: looks solid, I'll skip this and what it builds on. On a miss, two of four, the wrong pairs turn red, and it says: no problem, I'll keep this in your plan. Either way you get the explanation and a Continue button. No question is thrown away anymore, zero skipped, down from a hundred eighty-six.

beats.narration_text: What's honest about it. The scorer, the gate branch, and the app self-check are built and tested, sixty-two tests pass, a hundred seventy-eight items are live, and nothing is skipped. But the seventy-five percent bar is a chosen default, not a verified one. The questions are borrowed from our collaborators' bank and held out of the repo, and one chapter-two title still doesn't match. And eight items came through malformed, a bank defect, not a textbook problem. The content is sound, so I recovered all eight into a separate review file and kept them out of the live pipeline until Evin confirms them. Built and tested, but not yet verified.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're scoring a structured answer, grade it by its parts, relational partial credit, not all-or-nothing, and keep the raw fraction so a richer model can use it later. Separate the signal from the stakes: let a check inform advancement while staying opt-in and formative, never a grade. And when source data comes in broken but sound, recover it into a separate file instead of throwing it away, and keep it aside until an expert signs off.
